summary:
We developed a web-based platform that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS active fire detections into a consistent monthly hotspot time series for Paraguay, covering November 2000 to November 2026. The project addresses the challenge of combining observations from different satellite sensors, whose spatial resolutions, detection characteristics, and operational periods differ, making long-term fire analysis difficult.

Our approach processes FIRMS satellite data, aggregates detections onto a common 0.25° spatial grid, and applies a calibration methodology to produce a MODIS-equivalent harmonized series. We also assess the consistency of the conversion, quantify its uncertainty, and explore the use of the resulting time series for experimental forecasting with an N-HiTS deep learning model.

The project provides an accessible interactive Streamlit application for exploring the data and visualizing the results. By creating a more consistent historical record, our work supports long-term wildfire monitoring, trend analysis, and data-driven decision-making. This is particularly important for Paraguay, where wildfires pose significant threats to ecosystems, biodiversity, agricultural activities, and local communities.
details:
Project Details

Our project develops an interactive platform to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspot observations into a consistent monthly time series for Paraguay, covering November 2000 to November 2026.

How it works: The system processes active-fire detections obtained from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). It applies consistent confidence and fire-type filters, assigns detections to a common 0.25° spatial grid, and aggregates them monthly. Since MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection characteristics, we apply a month-specific calibration factor to convert VIIRS observations into MODIS-equivalent hotspot counts. The resulting dataset includes uncertainty estimates, data-source information, and reliability flags to distinguish estimated, validated, and provisional periods.

Benefits and intended impact: The platform provides a more consistent historical record of fire activity, reducing artificial discontinuities caused by changes in satellite sensors. It enables users to explore spatial and temporal patterns, compare different periods, and better understand the limitations of the observations. Our goal is to support researchers, environmental organizations, and decision-makers working on wildfire monitoring, ecosystem protection, and land management in Paraguay.

Technologies and tools: We used Python as the main programming language, Jupyter Notebook for data processing and analysis, and libraries such as Pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib. Streamlit was used to develop the interactive web application, while GitHub provides version control and project hosting. The project relies on publicly available NASA FIRMS satellite observations from MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua, and VIIRS Suomi-NPP. No custom satellite hardware was required.

Creativity and design considerations: The main innovation is not simply combining two satellite datasets, but developing a transparent conversion methodology that makes observations from different sensors comparable over a much longer period. We considered spatial resolution, sensor overlap, seasonal variations, detection confidence, temporal consistency, missing observations, and uncertainty. We also prioritized accessibility by creating a web interface that allows users to explore the results without needing programming skills.

AI-assisted tools (Claude) were used to support parts of the coding, debugging, and documentation process. The project methodology, data processing decisions, validation approach, and interpretation of results were reviewed as part of the development process.
